\section[\ml{നായ}, \ml{പൂച്ച}]{\ml{നായ}, \ml{പൂച്ച} — matching Tamil closely on both counts}

\label{lesson:ML-C21-naaya-poocha}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Malayalam keeps close company with its nearest cousin, Tamil, on both words this time — while still fitting into the honest, more fragmented Dravidian picture for "cat."
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\textbf{\ml{നായ}} (\emph{nāya}, "\textbf{dog}") continues the same solid, native \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} root as Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ನಾಯಿ}} (\emph{nāyi}) and Tamil's own word — no mystery here at all, unlike every dog-word you've met elsewhere in this entire arc.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{പൂച്ച}} (\emph{pūcha}, "\textbf{cat}") closely matches Tamil's \textbf{everyday} word for cat — a different root from Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ಬೆಕ್ಕು}} (\emph{bekku}, related instead to the word for "wildcat") and Telugu's \textbf{\te{పిల్లి}} (\emph{pilli}, a separate Proto-Dravidian root of its own, most likely the source behind Sanskrit's \emph{biḍāla} and Hindi's \emph{billī}). So "cat" genuinely splits three ways across just these four Dravidian languages, even though "dog" mostly agrees.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "nāya" — dog, same solid root as Kannada and Tamil{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "pūcha" — cat, matching Tamil's everyday word closely{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Does \textbf{\ml{നായ}} share Kannada's \emph{nāyi} root? (\textbf{Yes} — the same solid, native Proto-Dravidian root.) Does \textbf{\ml{പൂച്ച}} match Kannada's \emph{bekku} or Tamil's everyday cat-word? (\textbf{Tamil's} — Kannada's \emph{bekku} and Telugu's \emph{pilli} both come from different roots entirely.)
\end{tcolorbox}
